title: "Economic Satisfaction, Income and Wealth"
format: html
---

This report compares country-year summaries of satisfaction with the state of
the economy (ESS `stfeco`) with distributional series from the World Inequality
Database (WID). Country-year comparisons require observations of satisfaction,
income and wealth, and the validity rules below apply throughout the analysis.



## Data Validity

An observation is valid for comparison only when ESS flags the country-year as
reliable, both WID distributions contain all ten equal-split adult decile shares
and sum to one within 2.5 percentage points, and neither WID series marks the
year as extrapolated. The WID metadata does not identify all interpolated years.
Observations failing any rule are excluded from every section after
comparability.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Validity check                 | Passing country-years| Matched country-years|
|:------------------------------|---------------------:|---------------------:|
|Satisfaction estimate reliable |                   267|                   369|
|Complete valid wealth deciles  |                   369|                   369|
|Wealth not extrapolated        |                   369|                   369|
|Complete valid income deciles  |                   369|                   369|
|Income not extrapolated        |                   307|                   369|
|Pass all validity checks       |                   225|                   369|


:::
:::

## Satisfaction and Income/Wealth Association

The merged table uses the earliest matched observation in each two-year ESS
round and the corresponding WID distribution. It retains ESS reliability,
effective sample size, the selected post-tax income series where available,
and WID extrapolation flags. The full country-round table is available as
[data/processed/ess_wid_country_round.csv](data/processed/ess_wid_country_round.csv).

All summaries and correlations below use ESS observations flagged reliable.
Correlations are descriptive only; no significance tests are performed. Gini
values are approximated from WID's ten decile shares. Palma is the top 10% share
divided by the bottom 40% share; wealth Palma is missing when bottom-40 net wealth
is zero or negative.

### Selected Correlation Scatterplots

These pooled country-round comparisons show the three distribution metrics in each
domain with the largest absolute Spearman correlations. Each metric is paired with
its strongest selected satisfaction summary. Wealth middle-40% and income bottom-50%
shares are always included when a usable pairing exists. The table identifies the
actual measures selected; share axes are percentages.

Selection is exploratory, not evidence of statistical significance or causation.
Countries contribute repeated observations, so these pooled correlations combine
between-country differences with changes over time. Each point is a reliable
country-round; red lines are descriptive ordinary least-squares fits.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}

## Income and Wealth Distribution Change

This section summarizes annualized income and wealth distribution changes for
countries with matched economic satisfaction data. Years use two-year survey rounds
anchored at 2002; the earliest matched observation in each round is used. Each
reported transition compares consecutive selected survey observations, skipping
intervening distribution years. WID post-tax national-income shares are used where
available, with pre-tax shares as a fallback. For each transition, the score is
the mean absolute change across the nine cumulative decile-share cutoffs,
divided by the gap between survey observations. It is a magnitude in percentage
points per year; it does not indicate whether inequality rose or fell. The
metric uses the cumulative share profile directly, so it also applies when net
wealth shares are negative.

### Satisfaction Change Against Distribution Change

These transition-level comparisons relate the annualized absolute satisfaction mean
change to the annualized income or wealth distribution-change magnitude.
Same-interval comparisons match identical endpoint years. Lagged comparisons match both distribution endpoints 3 survey rounds earlier than the satisfaction endpoints; missing rounds are not skipped.
Only reliable satisfaction
transitions and non-extrapolated distribution transitions are included. Both measures
are magnitudes, so these associations do not show whether satisfaction or
inequality rose or fell. Correlations are descriptive.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|concept |alignment                     |   n| pearson| spearman|
|:-------|:-----------------------------|---:|-------:|--------:|
|income  |Same interval                 | 153|    0.17|     0.11|
|wealth  |Same interval                 | 153|    0.17|     0.12|
|income  |Distribution 3 rounds earlier |  69|   -0.02|    -0.04|
|wealth  |Distribution 3 rounds earlier |  69|   -0.10|    -0.01|

Each point is a country, positioned by its median annualized change for wealth

### Largest Income and Wealth Changes

The top transitions are ranked by annualized magnitude and use consecutive survey

::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](figures/descriptive/distribution_change/wid/largest_changes.png){width=900}

## Economic Satisfaction Change

Satisfaction changes are calculated from the survey summaries. The mean measures
movement in average satisfaction with the state of the economy; the IQR measures
change in spread. Both are annualized absolute changes in satisfaction scale points.
Years use two-year survey rounds anchored at 2002, with the earliest available
valid matched observation in each round. Transitions compare consecutive selected
observations; gaps may span more than one round.

### Largest Satisfaction Mean and IQR Changes

The largest mean changes are ranked by annualized magnitude. The IQR panel shows
the observed IQR at both survey endpoints for the largest annualized IQR changes,
making the before/after spread visible. Segment color indicates whether the IQR
widened or narrowed; an asterisk marks an unreliable or unclassified endpoint.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](figures/descriptive/distribution_change/ess/largest_changes.png){width=950}
